samples.text:
The diagram shows how the old smartphones are recycled. There are eight stages in this process.

First, people return their phones to the shops or send them by post. Then all the personal data on the phones is erased. After that, the phones are tested. If the phone is working, it is repaired and sold again to other people.

The faulty phones go to the next stage, it is dismantling. In this stage, the battery and the screen is removed. Then the battery is recycled and lithium and cobalt are recovered from it. The remaining parts of the phone are shredded into small pieces.

After the shredding, the metals like gold, silver and copper are extracted. Finally, all the materials are sold to manufacturers so they can use it again.

Overall, the process begins with the drop-off of old phones and ends with the reuse of materials. Some phones is repaired and sold again, but the others are broken into parts to get the metals and other materials from them.
samples.why: Overview late and simple · both routes and all stages covered in order · mechanical linking · some informal vocabulary · agreement and article errors and a comma splice, meaning always clear.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the process by which old smartphones are recycled, either by being reused as phones or by being broken down for their materials.

Overall, the process has eight stages, beginning with phones being dropped off and ending with materials being sold to manufacturers. A key feature is that phones which still work are repaired and resold, whereas faulty ones are taken apart so that their materials can be recovered.

At the start, phones are returned either to shops or by post, and all personal data is erased from them. They are then tested, and those that are working are repaired and sold again, so they do not continue to the later stages. Faulty phones, however, are dismantled, with the battery and the screen being removed.

After that, the batteries are recycled so that lithium and cobalt can be recovered, while the remaining parts of the phones are shredded. From this shredded material, three metals, namely gold, silver and copper, is extracted. In the final stage, all of these recovered materials are sold to manufacturers, who can reuse them to make new products.
samples.why: Clear overview identifying the two routes · logical progression with contrast and sequence linkers · appropriate vocabulary (dismantled, recovered, faulty) · mostly error-free with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The diagram outlines how old smartphones are processed for recycling, from the moment they are handed in to the point at which their materials re-enter manufacturing.

Of the eight stages, testing is pivotal, since it determines which of two routes a phone will take: working devices are repaired and resold, while faulty ones are dismantled and broken down so that their constituent materials can be recovered and sold on.

Phones are first returned, either to shops or by post, after which all personal data stored on them is wiped. They are then tested, and those found to be in working order are repaired and put back on the market. Defective handsets, by contrast, are dismantled, with the battery and screen being removed. Notably, both routes begin only after the data-wiping stage, so no phone is tested while it still holds personal information.

The batteries are recycled to recover lithium and cobalt, whereas the remaining components are shredded. Gold, silver and copper are then extracted from this shredded material. Finally, all of the recovered materials are sold to manufacturers for reuse, which brings the process to an end.
samples.why: Skilful overview focusing on the decisive testing stage · both routes traced accurately · precise vocabulary (pivotal, constituent, defective) · wide range of complex and passive structures · error-free.
